title: cvcs succession shocker is shrewder than it looks 2026 09 09
author: Liam Proud
text:
LONDON, Sept 9 (Reuters Breakingviews) - Private-capital managers almost always find their bosses from within. Each firm thinks its culture confers unique advantages. Meanwhile, poaching top talent is complicated when so much pay is locked away in ​performance-linked carried interest. CVC Capital Partners (CVC.AS)
, opens new tab
, with €212 billion of assets under management, bucked the trend on Wednesday by naming
, opens new tab
 TPG's Todd Sisitsky ‌as co-CEO alongside internal highflyer Peter Rutland. There are many surprising things about the move, though it just about makes sense.
The first oddity is that Sisitsky has a reputation as an American buyout specialist, whereas CVC's private-equity business is more focused on the other side of the Atlantic. A 2023 marketing presentation
, opens new tab
 showed that the U.S. accounted for ​just 18% of the capital committed by the Amsterdam-listed group's flagship fund at the time. The group's 2025 annual report noted ​that clients, including major American pension plans, value CVC's "strong European heritage". Hiring an American as co-CEO doesn't obviously fit.
Nor ⁠is it clear, from Wednesday's statement, specifically what Sisitsky and Rutland will respectively be in charge of. The latter, a Brit with an expertise ​in financial services, is currently responsible for the non-buyout parts of the group: credit and insurance, secondaries, and infrastructure. If that division of labour persists, ​it would logically follow that Sisitsky's domain will include private equity. That would make the geographic mismatch all the more striking.
Another risk is organ rejection, which is heightened by the fact that the firm has an idiosyncratic culture. Carried interest, or the 20% of the upside that managers keep for running a fund, is partly allocated on ​a deal-by-deal basis at CVC. This pay policy, at best, fosters accountability among the investing teams. Yet it's unusually Darwinian compared with other firms, which ​have a higher emphasis on pooled carry, where the risks and rewards are mutualised. This unique structure could be harder for an outsider to navigate.
Founder-chair Rolly van ‌Rappard at ⁠least has a long time to explain himself, since the changes will only take effect by the first quarter of 2028. It's possible to imagine how he will set any fears to rest. First, CVC has a good track record of bringing in outsiders. Many of its senior partners, like Alex Dibelius in Germany and Cathrin Petty in New York, joined after long careers elsewhere.
Second, having an American co-CEO doesn't have to mean radically shifting ​the private-equity investment focus. Two people ​familiar with the company's thinking told ⁠Breakingviews on Wednesday that there were no plans to increase the percentage of its flagship funds that go towards U.S. assets.
Still, if van Rappard were to decide to become more American over time, that might not be ​a bad thing for shareholders. CVC’s shares are slightly below the 2024 initial public offering. One possible solution is ​to boost growth ⁠by launching more funds in the world's biggest market, or even buying up new expertise, as seen in the recent acquisition
, opens new tab
 of credit specialist Marathon Asset Management. Hiring a veteran U.S. dealmaker may be the quickest way for CVC to fill a critical gap.
